info.bio: Sex Pistols fue una emblemática e influyente banda de punk rock activa durante la primera ola del punk británica. Durante su fugaz existencia, desde 1975 hasta 1979 en la que editaron tan solo cuatro sencillos y un álbum, se convirtió en la espina dorsal del género en Inglaterra y su simple existencia motivó la formación de cientos de otros grupos. Los Pistols son acreditados frecuentemente como los iniciadores del movimiento punk en el Reino Unido y los creadores de la primera brecha generacional en el rock and roll.

scenes.name: Punk rock (1976-77)
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: El «Año Cero»: hacia el verano de 1977 el punk ya era una parodia de sí mismo y su frágil alianza entre chicos obreros y bohemios de escuela de arte se rompe. De un lado quedan los «punks verdaderos», populistas, que desembocarán en el Oi! y el hardcore; del otro, la vanguardia que se llamará postpunk, que vio en 1977 no un retorno al rock crudo sino la ocasión de romper con la tradición. Su legado común: la fe en el poder de la música y el «hazlo tú mismo».

scenes.name: Malcolm McLaren y Bow Wow Wow
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: Tras perder a los Sex Pistols, McLaren se exilia en París, descubre la música africana y, con la moda pirata del siglo XVIII de Vivienne Westwood, concibe su contraataque al postpunk «para universitarios»: ritmos burundeses (Simon Jeffes enseña polirritmia a Adam and the Ants, a quienes luego roba la banda), glamour, sexualidad adolescente y piratería en cassette. Con la anglobirmana Annabella Lwin, de catorce años, nace Bow Wow Wow: «C·30 C·60 C·90 Go!» (1980), Your Cassette Pet, solo en cassette con caja de cigarrillos, «W.O.R.K.» (el paro como liberación: «conviértanse en piratas»). Anticipa el walkman, la world music y la música como banda sonora portátil, pero también manipula y explota a sus músicos (la revista nunca editada Chicken, fotos con menores). See Jungle! (1982) es una obra maestra del pop justo cuando él pierde el interés; «I Want Candy» triunfa en Estados Unidos. Boy George pasa brevemente por el grupo antes de fundar Culture Club.

scenes.name: Punk-rock británico
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La gira de los Ramones de 1976 contagia a Inglaterra, donde el punk es combinación de moda y paro: la Gran Bretaña de Thatcher, con las ciudades industriales devastadas, convierte el «punk» en algo mucho más serio que lo que pretendían los Ramones. Malcolm McLaren inventa el sonido (Sex Pistols, «los Ramones con heroína y valium») y la imagen. The Clash, los más intelectuales (London Calling, Sandinista); Damned, Generation X, Buzzcocks (inventores del punk-pop), Vibrators. En Australia, Radio Birdman y los Saints. La segunda ola (GBH, UK Subs, Neurotics, New Model Army, Stiff Little Fingers) y el punk anarquista (Crass, Discharge, Rudimentari Peni, Subhumans).

podcast.title: Formation and Johnny Rotten's Audition (1975)
podcast.body: In 1975, Malcolm McLaren, the former manager of The New York Dolls and co-proprietor of the "Sex" clothing shop at 430 King's Road in London's Chelsea area, sought to form a band as a living advertisement for his store. He liked the name "Pistols" for its dangerous connotation, thus "Sex Pistols." Malcolm was looking for a singer and was introduced to 19-year-old Johnny Lydon (later Johnny Rotten), who had green teeth and was spotted by Bernie Rhodes wearing a homemade "I hate Pink Floyd" t-shirt held together with safety pins. Despite Lydon's inability to sing, Malcolm had him audition by miming and "singing" Alice Cooper's "I'm 18" to a jukebox in the shop, which landed him the role. "So Malcolm got young John to audition, not caring if Johnny could actually sing a note, which he couldn't."

McLaren assembled the group using "snotty kids" who frequented his store, naming them "Sex" after his shop and "Pistols" because it sounded dangerous.

They embodied the rage of Britain's underemployed young working class, expressing disdain for the monarchy and hatred for the social order and class system. Their snotty attitude, shocking dress, and aggressive music made them a "clear and present danger" to UK society. "Back then in 75, 76, they were considered to be seriously dangerous to everybody."

podcast.title: "Today" Show Interview (1976) – National Controversy
podcast.body: On Wednesday, December 1st, 1976, the Sex Pistols appeared on the popular UK tea-time chat show *Today*, hosted by Bill Grundy. They were a last-minute replacement for Queen, who had to cancel due to Freddie Mercury's throat infection. The band and their entourage consumed a bottle of Blue Nun in the limo and more liquor in the green room before going on live, unaware the show was unedited. Grundy's provocative questioning led to the band using profanity on air, which resulted in Grundy's two-week suspension, the producer and director's firing, and widespread media outrage with headlines like "the filth and the fury." This 117-second incident, despite being accidental, massively boosted punk rock's profile in the UK, causing "Anarchy in the UK" sales to jump from 10,000 copies in a week to 10,000 copies a day. "The impact of that 117 second interview was immediate."

podcast.title: Sid Vicious Ashes Allegedly Spilled at Heathrow Terminal 4 (February 1979)
podcast.body: After Sid Vicious's death on February 2, 1979 (heroin overdose while awaiting trial for the murder of Nancy Spungen), his mother Anne Beverly had him cremated. Two weeks later, allegedly drunk while returning to London through Heathrow Airport, she tripped, fell, and spilled Sid's ashes in the terminal — some reportedly embedded in the carpet and sucked into the ventilation system. Rumor holds that Sid Dust still circulates through Terminal 4. However, those with knowledge say this is not what happened: what is confirmed is that before returning to England, Anne took his ashes to Nancy Spungen's grave in Philadelphia and spread them there. What is also confirmed is that New York police tipped off London police, who raided Anne's Notting Hill home, found drugs, and arrested her. Anne Beverly died on September 6, 1996, after carefully putting her affairs in order and then consuming a large quantity of painkillers, tranquilizers, and alcohol. "Rumor has it that Sid Dust still circulates throughout terminal four."

podcast.title: "Bollocks" Obscenity Controversy
podcast.body: The word "ballocks" on the album cover was deemed obscene by some upon its release, leading to significant problems for record stores and radio stations. In London, police visited Virgin Record stores displaying the album poster, threatening prosecution under the 1889 Indecent Advertisements Act. This led to managers removing posters and at least one store manager being arrested. The controversy escalated when the story hit newspapers before the album's release, prompting ads like "The album will last, the sleeve may not." A court case on November 24, 1977, involved expert witnesses, including an English professor, testifying that "ballocks" was an old English term for priest or, in context, meant "nonsense." Everyone involved was ultimately found not guilty, and the album became highly influential. "The word ballocks was deemed obscene by some, which caused all sorts of issues for record stores in radio."

podcast.title: Nancy Spungen's Murder and Sid Vicious's Arrest
podcast.body: Nancy Spungen died on October 12th, 1978, from a single knife wound to her abdomen after a party in their Chelsea Hotel room the previous night, October 11th. Sid Vicious had taken 22 tablets of a powerful sedative and passed out, only to wake up to find Nancy dead on the bathroom floor, covered in congealed blood. The autopsy determined she bled to death over at least three hours. The murder weapon was a 007 hunting knife Sid had purchased on 42nd Street, inspired by Steve Bator's of the Dead Boys. podcast.title: Sid Vicious's Death and Ashes Disposition
podcast.body: Sid Vicious died of a heroin overdose in his sleep in the early morning hours of February 2nd, 1979, at 63 Bank Street in Greenwich Village, New York, while out on bail awaiting trial for the death of Nancy Spungen. A legend, though unproven, suggests he died with a note asking to be buried next to Nancy in his leather jacket, jeans, and motorcycle boots. Another popular, but false, myth claims his mother, Beverly, spilled his ashes at Heathrow Airport. Semi-reliable sources claim his ashes never left America, with his mother reportedly taking them to King David Cemetery in Philadelphia, where Nancy was buried, hopping a fence to dump them on Nancy's grave against her parents' wishes. podcast.title: Sid Vicious's On-Tour Conduct
podcast.body: During the American tour, Sid Vicious was notoriously problematic, spitting at people and instigating fights with anyone who looked at him in a way he perceived as offensive. He famously used his bass guitar to swing "like a cricket bat at people's heads." His behavior was so extreme that he was even beaten up by his own bodyguard a few days into the tour. Due to his drug use, he was considered "too stupider to stone to actually play," so his amplifier was never actually hooked up, with a roadie offstage playing all his bass parts. "Sid Vicious wasn't much help. He spit at everybody and he picked fights with anyone who looked at him funny."

podcast.title: Sid Vicious's Pogo Invention
podcast.body: Sid Vicious, who later became the bassist for the Sex Pistols, is credited in legend as the inventor of the Pogo dance. He reportedly started pogoing to mock non-punks who attended the band's shows, as he felt they didn't truly belong. Another account from Shane McGowan suggests Sid's tight leather poncho restricted his dance movements to just jumping. "legend says he started Pogoing as a way of mocking non-punks who came to see the pistols."

podcast.title: Sid Vicious's Subsequent Jailing and Death
podcast.body: After being bailed out following Nancy Spungen's murder charge, Sid Vicious was re-jailed for 55 days for slashing a man's face with a broken beer bottle. He was bailed out again before the murder case could proceed to trial, but he died of an overdose. "He stayed there for 55 days before he was bailed out again. But before the case could come to trial, Sid died of an overdose."

podcast.title: Subversive US Tour Strategy
podcast.body: Instead of hitting major markets, manager Malcolm McLaren designed a "subversive" strategy for the US tour, planning a major swing into the punk-unfriendly Southern US. This tour, however, "did not go well," with hostile crowds and Sid Vicious often being too strung out to perform effectively. "But instead of hitting all the major markets, McLaren thought it would be very subversive, very punk, if the pistols made a big swing into the punk, unfriendly, southern US."

xref.title: First Show October 17, 1975 – Pre-dates Sex Pistols and The Clash; 1980 Ontario Place Riot
xref.body: Teenage Head formed in Hamilton, Ontario, and played their first show on October 17, 1975 at Westdale High School — three weeks before the Sex Pistols played their first gig, and nine months before The Clash formed. They were a major force in Canadian punk, combining elements of the Ramones, New York Dolls, and 1950s rock and roll. Their profile peaked with a 1980 show at Ontario Place in Toronto where thousands tried to get in; what followed became an infamous riot. American radio programmers loved the music but balked at the band name (for obvious reasons), prompting a temporary rename to "Teenage Heads" for US purposes. Just before a crucial US showcase in September 1980, guitarist Gord Lewis was in a serious car accident, canceling the shows and closing the window of opportunity. Original singer Frankie Venom died of throat cancer in 2008; the band continues with Dave Rave on vocals more than 40 years later. "Long after most of their original punk rock contemporaries called it quits, or died off, Teenage Head still with us."

xref.title: "Today" Show Interview (1976) – National Controversy
xref.body: On Wednesday, December 1st, 1976, the Sex Pistols appeared on the popular UK tea-time chat show *Today*, hosted by Bill Grundy. They were a last-minute replacement for Queen, who had to cancel due to Freddie Mercury's throat infection. The band and their entourage consumed a bottle of Blue Nun in the limo and more liquor in the green room before going on live, unaware the show was unedited. Grundy's provocative questioning led to the band using profanity on air, which resulted in Grundy's two-week suspension, the producer and director's firing, and widespread media outrage with headlines like "the filth and the fury." This 117-second incident, despite being accidental, massively boosted punk rock's profile in the UK, causing "Anarchy in the UK" sales to jump from 10,000 copies in a week to 10,000 copies a day. "The impact of that 117 second interview was immediate."

xref.title: Bill Grundy TV Incident – December 1976
xref.body: Following their appearance with Bill Grundy on television in December 1976, the Sex Pistols became the recognizable face of punk rock in Britain. "And over the course of those two nights, July 4th and July 6th, 1976, just about every single person who would become a major player in the British punk rock explosion were taught a lesson by the Ramones."

"This two minutes has gone down in history as one of the most legendary rock and roll television appearances ever."

xref.title: Disastrous American Tour – January 1978
xref.body: Manager Malcolm McLaren's plan to "conquer America" with the Sex Pistols resulted in one of rock history's most disastrous road trips. Initially, the group's visa applications were denied, forcing them to cancel an important appearance on Saturday Night Live, where Elvis Costello was called in as a last-minute replacement. The drummer for Elvis Costello's performance notably wore a t-shirt that read "Thanks, milk," a sarcastic jab at Malcolm McLaren. McLaren made a bizarre miscalculation about American culture by routing the tour away from major cities and through the deep South, an area not receptive to punk rock values. "Instead, what he got was one of the most disastrous road trips in the history of rock."

xref.title: Involvement in Nancy Spungen's Death (October 12, 1978)
xref.body: Sid Vicious, bassist for the Sex Pistols, was implicated in the death of his girlfriend, Nancy Spungen, who was found stabbed to death in room 100 of the Chelsea Hotel in New York on October 12, 1978. Sid and Nancy were both heroin and Tuinal addicts, and on the night of her death, Sid reportedly took up to 52 Tuinal tablets, which would have rendered him unconscious. Although he initially confessed, his level of incapacitation made it unlikely he remembered. He was arrested and charged with Nancy's murder but died of a heroin overdose before the trial could commence. "Sid was arrested, charged with Nancy's murder, and then died of a heroin overdose before things could go to trial."

xref.title: Litigation and Control (1978-1987)
